title: How to hear this sermon
english: This is a listening version of John Wesley's sermon, Upon Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse Two. It is the sermon as printed in John Wesley's 1771 Works. Rendered in modern English.

title: Blessed are the meek
english: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Matthew 5:5.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled. Matthew 5:6.
Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Matthew 5:7.

title: When the mourner is comforted
english: When the winter is past, when the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in the land, when he who comforts the mourners has now returned, so that he may stay with them for ever, when at the brightness of his presence the clouds disperse, the dark clouds of doubt and uncertainty, the storms of fear flee away, the waves of sorrow subside, and their spirit again rejoices in God their Savior, then this word is eminently fulfilled. Then those whom he has comforted can bear witness: Blessed, or happy, are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.

title: Who are the meek
english: But who are the meek? Not those who grieve at nothing because they know nothing, who are not disturbed by the evils that occur because they cannot tell evil from good. Not those who are sheltered from the shocks of life by a stupid insensibility, who have, either by nature or by art, the virtue of stocks and stones, and resent nothing because they feel nothing. Brute philosophers have nothing to do with this. Apathy is as far from meekness as it is from humanity. So one would not easily conceive how any Christians of the purer ages, especially any of the fathers of the church, could confuse these, and mistake one of the foulest errors of heathenism for a branch of true Christianity.

Nor does Christian meekness mean being without zeal for God, any more than it means ignorance or insensibility. No. It keeps clear of every extreme, whether too much or too little. It does not destroy the affections. It balances them. The God of nature never meant that grace should root them out, but only that they should be brought and kept under due regulation. It sets the mind right. It holds an even scale with regard to anger, and sorrow, and fear, keeping the mean in every circumstance of life, and not leaning either to the right hand or to the left.

title: Toward God, ourselves, and our neighbor
english: Meekness, then, seems properly to relate to ourselves. But it may be referred either to God or to our neighbor. When this due composure of mind has reference to God, it is usually called resignation: a calm acceptance of whatever is his will concerning us, even though it may not please nature, saying continually, It is the Lord. Let him do what seems good to him (1 Samuel 3:18). When we consider it more strictly with regard to ourselves, we call it patience, or contentment. When it is exercised toward other people, then it is mildness to the good, and gentleness to the evil.

title: They can see evil and suffer it
english: Those who are truly meek can clearly see what is evil, and they can also suffer it. They feel everything of this kind, but still meekness holds the reins. They are exceedingly zealous for the Lord of hosts, but their zeal is always guided by knowledge, and tempered, in every thought and word and work, with the love of man as well as the love of God. They do not desire to put out any of the passions which God has, for wise ends, planted in their nature. But they have the mastery of them all. They hold them all in subjection, and use them only in service of those ends. And so even the harsher and more unpleasant passions are fit for the noblest purposes. Even hate, and anger, and fear, when engaged against sin, and regulated by faith and love, are like walls and bulwarks to the soul, so that the wicked one cannot come near to hurt it.

title: It must increase
english: It is plain that this divine temper is not only to remain, but to increase in us day by day. Occasions of exercising it, and so of increasing it, will never be wanting while we remain on earth. We need patience, so that after we have done and suffered the will of God, we may receive the promise. We need resignation, so that we may in all circumstances say, Not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39). And we need gentleness toward all people, but especially toward the evil and the unthankful. Otherwise we shall be overcome by evil, instead of overcoming evil with good (Romans 12:21).

title: Not only the outward act
english: Nor does meekness restrain only the outward act, as the scribes and Pharisees taught of old, and as the miserable teachers who are not taught by God will not fail to do in every age. Our Lord guards against this, and shows the true extent of meekness, in the following words. You have heard that it was said by those of old, You shall not kill, and whoever kills shall be in danger of the judgment. Matthew 5:21.

But I say to you that whoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment, and whoever says to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council. But whoever says, You fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

title: Anger in the heart
english: Our Lord here ranks under the head of murder even that anger which goes no further than the heart, which does not show itself by any outward unkindness, no, not so much as a passionate word.

Whoever is angry with his brother, with any living person, since we are all brothers and sisters, whoever feels any unkindness in his heart, any temper contrary to love, whoever is angry without a cause, without a sufficient cause, or further than that cause requires, shall be in danger of the judgment. He shall in that moment be exposed to the righteous judgment of God.

title: Without a cause
english: But would one not be inclined to prefer the reading of those copies which omit the word "without a cause"? Is it not entirely unnecessary? For if anger at persons is a temper contrary to love, how can there be a cause, a sufficient cause, for it, any cause that will justify it in the sight of God?

title: Anger at sin
english: Anger at sin we allow. In this sense we may be angry and yet not sin (Ephesians 4:26). In this sense our Lord himself is once recorded to have been angry. He looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardness of their hearts (Mark 3:5). He was grieved at the sinners, and angry at the sin. And this is undoubtedly right before God.

title: Raca
english: And whoever says to his brother, Raca, whoever gives way to anger so as to utter any contemptuous word. Commentators observe that Raca is a Syriac word which properly means empty, vain, foolish, so that it is as inoffensive an expression as can well be used toward someone with whom we are displeased. And yet whoever uses this, as our Lord assures us, shall be in danger of the council. Rather, he shall be exposed to it. He shall be liable to a severer sentence from the Judge of all the earth.

title: You fool
english: But whoever says, You fool. Whoever so gives place to the devil as to break out into reviling, into language meant to reproach and insult, shall be exposed to hell fire, and shall in that instant be liable to the highest condemnation. It should be observed that our Lord describes all of these as exposed to capital punishment. The first, to strangling, usually inflicted on those who were condemned in one of the lower courts. The second, to stoning, which was often inflicted on those who were condemned by the great council at Jerusalem. The third, to burning alive, inflicted only on the highest offenders, in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, the name from which the word we translate "hell" is plainly taken.

title: No commuting with God
english: And whereas people naturally imagine that God will excuse their failure in some duties because of their exactness in others, our Lord next takes care to cut off that vain, though common, imagination. He shows that it is impossible for any sinner to bargain with God, who will not accept one duty in place of another, or take a part of obedience for the whole. He warns us that doing our duty to God will not excuse us from our duty to our neighbor, that works of piety, as they are called, will be so far from commending us to God if we are lacking in love, that on the contrary that lack of love will make all those works an abomination to the Lord.

Therefore, if you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, because of your unkind behavior toward him, because of your calling him Raca, or You fool, do not think that your gift will atone for your anger, or that it will find any acceptance with God, so long as your conscience is stained with the guilt of unrepented sin. Leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, or at least do all that lies in you toward being reconciled, and then come and offer your gift. Matthew 5:23. Matthew 5:24.

title: Agree quickly
english: And let there be no delay in what so nearly concerns your soul. Agree with your adversary quickly. Now. On the spot. While you are on the way with him. If it is possible, before he goes out of your sight. Otherwise the adversary may at any time hand you over to the judge. Otherwise he may appeal to God, the Judge of all, and the Judge hand you over to the officer, to Satan, the executioner of the wrath of God, and you be thrown into prison, into hell, there to be kept for the judgment of the great day. Truly I say to you, you shall by no means come out of there until you have paid the last penny. But this you can never do, since you have nothing to pay. Therefore, if you are once in that prison, the smoke of your torment must go up for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11).

title: They shall inherit the earth
english: Meanwhile the meek shall inherit the earth. Such is the foolishness of worldly wisdom. The wise of the world had warned them again and again that if they did not resent such treatment, if they would quietly allow themselves to be abused in this way, there would be no living for them on earth, that they would never be able to get the common necessities of life, or even to keep what they had, that they could expect no peace, no quiet possession, no enjoyment of anything. Most true, if there were no God in the world, or if he did not concern himself with the children of men. But when God rises to judgment, and to help all the meek on earth, how he laughs all this heathen wisdom to scorn, and turns the fierceness of man to his praise. He takes particular care to provide them with everything needed for life and godliness. He secures to them the provision he has made, in spite of the force, fraud, or malice of men. And what he secures, he gives them richly to enjoy. It is sweet to them, whether little or much. As in patience they possess their souls, so they truly possess whatever God has given them. They are always content, always pleased with what they have. It pleases them because it pleases God. So that while their heart, their desire, their joy is in heaven, they may truly be said to inherit the earth.

title: The new earth
english: But there seems to be a further meaning in these words, even that they shall have a more eminent part in the new earth, where righteousness lives, in that inheritance of which Saint John has given a general description, and the details we shall know hereafter, in the twentieth chapter of the Revelation. And I saw an angel come down from heaven, and he laid hold of the dragon, that old serpent, and bound him for 1,000 years (Revelation 20:2). And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and of those who had not worshiped the beast, nor his image, nor received his mark on their foreheads or on their hands, and they lived and reigned with Christ for 1,000 years. But the rest of the dead did not live again until the 1,000 years were finished. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has part in the first resurrection. Over such the second death has no power. But they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him for 1,000 years.

title: The hindrances removed
english: Our Lord has so far been more immediately employed in removing the hindrances of true religion. Such is pride, the first great hindrance of all religion, which is taken away by poverty of spirit. Such are levity and thoughtlessness, which keep any religion from taking root in the soul until they are removed by holy mourning. Such are anger, impatience, and discontent, which are all healed by Christian meekness. And when once these hindrances are removed, these evil diseases of the soul, which were continually raising false cravings in it and filling it with sickly appetites, the native appetite of a heaven-born spirit returns. It hungers and thirsts after righteousness. And blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.

title: What righteousness is
english: Righteousness, as was observed before, is the image of God, the mind which was in Christ Jesus (Philippians 2:5). It is every holy and heavenly temper in one, springing from, as well as ending in, the love of God as our Father and Redeemer, and the love of all people for his sake.

title: The strongest appetite
english: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after this. To understand the expression fully, we should observe, first, that hunger and thirst are the strongest of all our bodily appetites. In the same way this hunger in the soul, this thirst after the image of God, is the strongest of all our spiritual appetites, once it is awakened in the heart. Yes, it swallows up all the rest in that one great desire, to be renewed after the likeness of him who created us (Colossians 3:10). We should observe, second, that from the time we begin to hunger and thirst, those appetites do not cease, but grow more and more craving and insistent, until we either eat and drink, or die. And even so, from the time we begin to hunger and thirst after the whole mind which was in Christ, these spiritual appetites do not cease, but cry after their food with more and more urgency. Nor can they possibly cease before they are satisfied, while any spiritual life remains. We may observe, third, that hunger and thirst are satisfied with nothing but food and drink. If you gave a hungry person all the world besides, all the elegance of clothing, all the trappings of state, all the treasure on earth, yes, thousands in gold and silver, if you paid him ever so much honor, he would not regard it. All these things are then of no account to him. He would still say, These are not the things I want. Give me food, or else I die. The very same is the case with every soul that truly hungers and thirsts after righteousness. He can find no comfort in anything but this. He can be satisfied with nothing else. Whatever else you offer, it is lightly esteemed. Whether it is riches, or honor, or pleasure, he still says, This is not the thing I want. Give me love, or else I die.

title: Not the religion of the world
english: And it is as impossible to satisfy such a soul, a soul that is thirsty for God, the living God (Psalm 42:2), with what the world calls religion, as with what the world calls happiness. The religion of the world means three things. First, doing no harm, abstaining from outward sin, at least from such as is scandalous, such as robbery, theft, common swearing, and drunkenness. Second, doing good, relieving the poor, being charitable, as it is called. Third, using the means of grace, at least going to church and to the Lord's Supper. The person in whom these three marks are found is called by the world a religious man. But will this satisfy the one who hungers after God? No. It is not food for his soul. He wants a religion of a nobler kind, a religion higher and deeper than this. He can no more feed on this poor, shallow, formal thing than he can fill his stomach with the east wind. True, he is careful to abstain from the very appearance of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:22). He is zealous for good works. He attends all the ordinances of God. But all this is not what he longs for. This is only the outside of that religion which he hungers after without ever being satisfied. The knowledge of God in Christ Jesus, the life which is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), being joined to the Lord in one Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:17), having fellowship with the Father and the Son (1 John 1:3), walking in the light as God is in the light (1 John 1:7), being purified even as he is pure (1 John 3:3): this is the religion, the righteousness, he thirsts after. Nor can he rest until he thus rests in God.

title: They shall be filled
english: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness in this way, for they shall be filled. They shall be filled with the thing they long for, even with righteousness and true holiness (Ephesians 4:24). God shall satisfy them with the blessings of his goodness, with the happiness of his chosen. He shall feed them with the bread of heaven, with the manna of his love. He shall give them to drink of his pleasures as from the river, and the one who drinks of it shall never thirst (John 4:14), except for more and more of the water of life (Revelation 22:17). This thirst shall last for ever.
The painful thirst, the fond desire, your joyful presence shall remove. But my full soul shall still require a whole eternity of love.

title: Do not lose the gift
english: Whoever you are, then, to whom God has given to hunger and thirst after righteousness, cry to him that you may never lose that gift beyond price, that this divine appetite may never cease. If many rebuke you and tell you to be quiet, do not regard them. Yes, cry out all the more, Jesus, Master, have mercy on me (Luke 17:13). Let me not live, except to be holy as you are holy (1 Peter 1:16). Spend no more of your money on what is not bread (Isaiah 55:2), nor your labor on what does not satisfy. Can you hope to dig happiness out of the earth, to find it in the things of the world? Oh, trample all its pleasures under foot. Despise its honors. Count its riches as dung and dross, yes, and all the things that are under the sun, for the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, for the entire renewal of your soul in that image of God in which it was first created. Beware of quenching that blessed hunger and thirst by what the world calls religion, a religion of form, of outward show, which leaves the heart as earthly and sensual as ever. Let nothing satisfy you but the power of godliness, a religion that is spirit and life, your dwelling in God and God in you, being an inhabitant of eternity, entering by the blood of sprinkling (Hebrews 12:24) within the veil, and sitting in the heavenly places with Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2:6).

title: Blessed are the merciful
english: And the more they are filled with the life of God, the more tenderly they will be concerned for those who are still without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12), still dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). Nor shall this concern for others lose its reward. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

The word used by our Lord more immediately means the compassionate, the tender-hearted, those who, far from despising them, earnestly grieve for those who do not hunger after God. This eminent part of brotherly love is here, by a common figure, put for the whole, so that the merciful, in the full sense of the term, are those who love their neighbors as themselves (Matthew 22:39).

title: Without love, nothing
english: Because of the vast importance of this love, without which, though we spoke with the tongues of men and of angels, though we had the gift of prophecy and understood all mysteries and all knowledge, though we had all faith so as to remove mountains, yes, though we gave all our goods to feed the poor, and our very bodies to be burned, it would profit us nothing, the wisdom of God has given us, by the apostle Paul, a full and particular account of it. By considering that account we shall most clearly see who the merciful are who shall obtain mercy.

title: Love suffers long
english: Love, for that is what one wishes the word had been rendered throughout, being a far plainer and less ambiguous word than charity, the love of our neighbor as Christ has loved us, suffers long (1 Corinthians 13:4). It is patient toward all people. It suffers all the weakness, ignorance, errors, and infirmities, all the stubbornness and littleness of faith, of the children of God, and all the malice and wickedness of the children of the world. And it suffers all this, not only for a time, for a short season, but to the end, still feeding our enemy when he hungers, and if he thirsts, still giving him drink, and so continually heaping coals of fire, of melting love, upon his head (Romans 12:20).

title: Love is kind
english: And in every step toward this desirable end, the overcoming of evil with good, love is kind. It is soft, mild, benign. It stands at the furthest distance from sullenness, from all harshness or sourness of spirit, and it inspires the one who suffers with, at once, the most amiable sweetness and the most fervent and tender affection.

title: Love does not envy
english: Consequently, love does not envy (1 Corinthians 13:4). It is impossible that it should. It is directly opposite to that poisonous temper. It cannot be that the person who has this tender affection for all, who earnestly wishes every temporal and spiritual blessing, every good thing in this world and in the world to come, to every soul that God has made, should be pained at his giving any good gift to any child of man. If he has himself received the same, he does not grieve, but rejoices, that another shares the common benefit. If he has not, he blesses God that his brother at least has it, and is in this happier than himself. And the greater his love, the more he rejoices in the blessings of all mankind, and the further he is removed from every kind and degree of envy toward any creature.

title: Love is not rash in judging
english: Love is not rash or hasty in judging. The phrase is not "does not vaunt itself," which would only repeat the very next words, but rather, as the word also properly means, is not rash or hasty in judging. It will not hastily condemn anyone. It does not pass a severe sentence on a slight or sudden view of things. It first weighs all the evidence, particularly the evidence brought in favor of the accused. A true lover of his neighbor is not like most people, who even in cases of the nicest nature see a little, presume a great deal, and so jump to the conclusion. No. He proceeds with caution and care, taking heed at every step, and willingly subscribes to that rule of the ancient heathen, and oh, where will the modern Christian appear: I am so far from lightly believing what one person says against another, that I will not easily believe what a person says against himself. I will always allow him second thoughts, and many times counsel too.

title: Love is not puffed up
english: It follows that love is not puffed up. It does not incline or allow anyone to think more highly of himself than he ought to think (Romans 12:3), but rather to think soberly. Yes, it humbles the soul to the dust. It destroys all high ideas that breed pride, and makes us rejoice to be as nothing, to be little and low, the lowest of all, the servant of all. Those who are kindly affectionate to one another with brotherly love cannot but, in honor, prefer one another. Those who, having the same love, are of one mind, do in lowliness of mind each esteem the other better than themselves (Philippians 2:3).

title: Love is not rude
english: It does not behave itself improperly. It is not rude, or willingly offensive to anyone. It gives everyone what is due: fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due, courtesy, civility, and humanity to all the world, honoring all people in their several degrees. A later writer defines good breeding, indeed the highest degree of it, politeness, as a continual desire to please, appearing in all one's behavior. But if so, no one is so well bred as a Christian, a lover of all mankind. For he cannot but desire to please all people, for their good, for their building up. And this desire cannot be hidden. It will necessarily appear in all his dealings with people. For his love is without pretense. It will appear in all his actions and conversation. Yes, and it will constrain him, though without deceit, to become all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22), if by any means he may save some.

title: Love does not seek its own
english: And in becoming all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22), love does not seek its own (1 Corinthians 13:5). In striving to please all people, the lover of mankind has no eye at all to his own temporal advantage. He covets no one's silver, or gold, or clothing. He desires nothing but the salvation of their souls. Yes, in some sense he may be said not to seek his own spiritual advantage any more than his temporal advantage. For while he is stretched to the full to save their souls from death, he, as it were, forgets himself. He does not think of himself, so long as that zeal for the glory of God swallows him up. Indeed, at some times he may almost seem, through an excess of love, to give up himself, both his soul and his body, while he cries out with Moses, Oh, this people have sinned a great sin. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin. And if not, blot me out of the book which you have written (Exodus 32:32). Or with Saint Paul, I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3).

title: Love is not provoked
english: It is no wonder that such love is not provoked. Let it be observed that the word "easily," strangely inserted in the translation, is not in the original. Saint Paul's words are absolute. Love is not provoked (1 Corinthians 13:5). It is not provoked to unkindness toward anyone. Occasions will indeed often occur, outward provocations of various kinds. But love does not yield to provocation. It triumphs over all. In all trials it looks to Jesus, and is more than conqueror in his love.

It is not unlikely that our translators inserted that word as if to excuse the apostle, who, as they supposed, might otherwise appear to be lacking in the very love he describes so beautifully. They seem to have supposed this from a phrase in the Acts of the Apostles, which is also translated very inaccurately. When Paul and Barnabas disagreed about John, the translation runs, And the contention was so sharp between them that they parted from one another. This naturally leads the reader to suppose that they were equally sharp in it, that Saint Paul, who was undoubtedly right with regard to the point in question, it being quite improper to take John with them again, who had deserted them before, was as much provoked as Barnabas, who gave such a proof of his anger as to leave the work for which he had been set apart by the Holy Spirit. But the original implies no such thing, nor does it say that Saint Paul was provoked at all. It simply says, And there was a sharpness, a fit of anger, in consequence of which Barnabas left Saint Paul, took John, and went his own way. Paul then chose Silas and departed, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God, which is not said of Barnabas, and he went through Syria and Cilicia, as he had proposed, strengthening the churches. But to return.

title: Love thinks no evil
english: Love prevents a thousand provocations which would otherwise arise, because it thinks no evil (1 Corinthians 13:5). Indeed the merciful person cannot avoid knowing many things that are evil. He cannot but see them with his own eyes and hear them with his own ears. For love does not put out his eyes, so that it is impossible for him not to see that such things are done. Neither does it take away his understanding, any more than his senses, so that he cannot but know that they are evil. For instance, when he sees a man strike his neighbor, or hears him blaspheme God, he cannot either question the thing done or the words spoken, or doubt that they are evil. Yet the word "thinks" does not refer either to our seeing and hearing, or to the first and involuntary acts of our understanding, but to our willingly thinking what we need not think, our inferring evil where it does not appear, our reasoning about things which we do not see, our supposing what we have neither seen nor heard. This is what true love absolutely destroys. It tears up, root and branch, all imagining of what we have not known. It casts out all jealousies, all evil suspicions, all readiness to believe evil. It is frank, open, unsuspicious, and as it cannot design evil, so neither does it fear it.

title: Love does not rejoice in iniquity
english: It does not rejoice in iniquity, common as this is even among those who bear the name of Christ, who do not scruple to rejoice over their enemy when he falls into affliction, or error, or sin. Indeed, how hard they can avoid this who are zealously attached to any party. How difficult it is for them not to be pleased with any fault they discover in those of the opposite party, with any real or supposed blemish, either in their principles or in their practice. What warm defender of any cause is clear of these? Yes, who is calm enough to be altogether free? Who does not rejoice when his adversary makes a false step which he thinks will advantage his own cause? Only a person of love. He alone weeps over either the sin or the folly of his enemy, takes no pleasure in hearing it or in repeating it, but rather desires that it may be forgotten for ever.

title: Love rejoices in the truth
english: But he rejoices in the truth, wherever it is found, in the truth which is according to godliness, bringing forth its proper fruit, holiness of heart and holiness of life. He rejoices to find that even those who oppose him, whether with regard to opinions or to some points of practice, are nevertheless lovers of God, and in other respects beyond reproach. He is glad to hear good of them, and to speak all he can consistently with truth and justice. Indeed, good in general is his glory and joy, wherever it is spread through the race of mankind. As a citizen of the world, he claims a share in the happiness of all its inhabitants. Because he is a man, he is not unconcerned in the welfare of any person, but enjoys whatever brings glory to God and promotes peace and good will among people.

title: Love covers all things
english: This love covers all things. So, without any doubt, the word should be translated, for otherwise it would be the very same as "endures all things." Because the merciful person does not rejoice in iniquity, neither does he willingly mention it. Whatever evil he sees, hears, or knows, he nevertheless conceals, so far as he can without making himself a sharer in other people's sins. Wherever he is, and with whomever he is, if he sees anything of which he does not approve, it does not go out of his lips, unless to the person concerned, in the hope that he may gain his brother. So far is he from making the faults or failings of others the matter of his conversation, that he never speaks of the absent at all, unless he can speak well. A tale-bearer, a backbiter, a whisperer, an evil-speaker, is to him the same as a murderer. He would just as soon cut his neighbor's throat as murder his reputation in this way. Just as soon would he think of amusing himself by setting fire to his neighbor's house, as of scattering abroad arrows, and firebrands, and death (Proverbs 26:18), and saying, Am I not joking?

He makes one exception only. Sometimes he is convinced that it is for the glory of God, or, which comes to the same thing, the good of his neighbor, that an evil should not be covered. In this case, for the benefit of the innocent, he is constrained to declare the guilty. But even here: first, he will not speak at all until love, a higher love, constrains him. Second, he cannot do it from a general, confused idea of doing good, or of promoting the glory of God, but from a clear sight of some particular end, some definite good which he pursues. Third, still he cannot speak unless he is fully convinced that this very means is necessary to that end, that the end cannot be reached, at least not so effectively, in any other way. Fourth, he then does it with the utmost sorrow and reluctance, using it as the last and worst medicine, a desperate remedy in a desperate case, a kind of poison never to be used except to drive out poison. Consequently, fifth, he uses it as sparingly as possible. And this he does with fear and trembling, lest he should break the law of love by speaking too much, more than he would have done by not speaking at all.

title: Love believes all things
english: Love believes all things. It is always willing to think the best, to put the most favorable construction on everything. It is always ready to believe whatever may tend to the advantage of anyone's character. It is easily convinced of what it earnestly desires, the innocence or integrity of any person, or at least of the sincerity of his repentance, if he once wandered from the way. It is glad to excuse whatever is wrong, to condemn the offender as little as possible, and to make all the allowance for human weakness which can be made without betraying the truth of God.

title: Love hopes all things
english: And when it can no longer believe, then love hopes all things. Is any evil reported of any person? Love hopes that the report is not true, that the thing reported was never done. Is it certain that it was? But perhaps it was not done in the circumstances that are reported, so that, allowing the fact, there is room to hope it was not so bad as it is represented. Was the action apparently and undeniably evil? Love hopes the intention was not so. Is it clear that the design was evil too? Yet might it not have sprung from a settled temper of the heart, but from a start of passion, or from some violent temptation, which hurried the person beyond himself? And even when it cannot be doubted that all the actions, designs, and tempers are equally evil, still love hopes that God will at last bare his arm and get himself the victory, and that there will be joy in heaven over this one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7), more than over ninety-nine just people who need no repentance.

title: Love endures all things
english: Lastly, it endures all things. This completes the character of the person who is truly merciful. He endures not some things, not many things only, not most, but absolutely all things. Whatever the injustice, the malice, the cruelty of people can inflict, he is able to suffer. He calls nothing intolerable. He never says of anything, This is not to be borne. No. He can not only do, but suffer, all things through Christ who strengthens him (Philippians 4:13). And all he suffers does not destroy his love, or impair it in the least. It is proof against all. It is a flame that burns even in the middle of the great deep. Many waters cannot quench his love (Song of Solomon 8:7), nor can the floods drown it. It triumphs over all. It never fails, either in time or in eternity.

In obedience to what heaven decrees, knowledge shall fail, and prophecy shall cease. But lasting love's more ample sway, neither bound by time nor subject to decay, in happy triumph shall for ever live, and endless good diffuse, and endless praise receive.

title: They shall obtain mercy
english: So the merciful shall obtain mercy, not only by the blessing of God on all their ways, by his now repaying the love they bear to their brothers and sisters a thousandfold into their own bosom, but also by an exceeding and eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17), in the kingdom prepared for them from the beginning of the world (Matthew 25:34).

title: How these Christians love
english: For a little while you may say, Woe is me, that I am constrained to live with Mesech, and to have my home among the tents of Kedar (Psalm 120:5). You may pour out your soul and lament the loss of true, genuine love on the earth. Lost indeed. You may well say, though not in the ancient sense, See how these Christians love one another. These Christian kingdoms, that are tearing out each other's bowels, desolating one another with fire and sword. These Christian armies, that are sending each other by thousands, and by tens of thousands, straight into hell. These Christian nations, that are all on fire with internal quarrels, party against party, faction against faction. These Christian cities, where deceit and fraud, oppression and wrong, yes, robbery and murder, do not leave their streets. These Christian families, torn apart with envy, jealousy, anger, and domestic quarrels, without number, without end. Yes, what is most dreadful, most to be lamented of all, these Christian churches. Churches, tell it not in Gath (2 Samuel 1:20), but alas, how can we hide it, either from Jews, Turks, or pagans, that bear the name of Christ, the Prince of peace, and wage continual war with each other. That convert sinners by burning them alive. That are drunk with the blood of the saints (Revelation 17:6). Does this charge belong only to Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots and of the abominations of the earth? No, truly. Reformed churches, so called, have learned well to follow in her steps. Protestant churches too know how to persecute, when they have power in their hands, even to blood. And meanwhile, how they also curse one another. They devote one another to the lowest hell. What wrath, what contention, what malice, what bitterness, is found everywhere among them, even where they agree in essentials and differ only in opinions, or in the outward details of religion. Who follows after only the things that make for peace, and the things by which one may build up another? Oh God, how long? Will your promise fail? Do not fear it, you little flock (Luke 12:32). Against hope, believe in hope (Romans 4:18). It is your Father's good pleasure still to renew the face of the earth. Surely all these things shall come to an end, and the inhabitants of the earth shall learn righteousness. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation (Isaiah 2:4), nor shall they learn war any more. The mountain of the Lord's house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and all the kingdoms of the world shall become the kingdom of our God. They shall not hurt or destroy in all his holy mountain (Isaiah 11:9), but they shall call their walls salvation and their gates praise. They shall all be without spot or blemish, loving one another, even as Christ has loved us. Be part of the first fruits, if the harvest is not yet. Love your neighbor as yourself. The Lord God fill your heart with such a love for every soul that you may be ready to lay down your life for his sake (John 15:13). May your soul continually overflow with love, swallowing up every unkind and unholy temper, until he calls you up into the region of love, there to reign with him for ever and ever.
